title: Your two bookends
hook: assemble a one-minute morning and a one-minute evening
tomorrow: up to us, not up to us

segments.voice: Yesterday: Franklin's chart, thirteen virtues and a dot for every slip. Your line was one virtue a week.

A shelf of books with nothing at either end. They lean, they slide, one falls, and the whole row goes down like dominoes. Put a heavy bookend at each side, and the same books stand straight all week. A day can be like that shelf. It starts with a phone alarm and a scroll, ends with a scroll and a phone alarm, and everything in between slumps. This week brought six ways to hold the ends. Today you choose two, one for each end, and make them yours.
screen: `A SHELF WITH NO ENDS.` → `EVERYTHING SLUMPS.` → `ONE BOOKEND AT EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week. For the morning: Marcus Aurelius at dawn, in the Meditations. Expect the busy-body and the ungrateful, remember they're your kin, and decide how you'll meet them. Your line was I'll meet them kindly. For the evening, four reviews. Seneca's teacher Sextius: what did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better? Seneca's own ledger, honest and then closed with a pardon: forgiven this time. The Golden Verses, credited to Pythagoras: where did I slip, what did I do, what did I leave undone? Ignatius of Loyola's examen: gratitude first, then the faults. And Franklin's chart, which added focus: one virtue a week. They don't all agree, and they don't need to. Ignatius prays; Seneca judges himself; Franklin keeps a chart. Each belongs to its own world. What they share is a shape: the day held at both ends, a look forward at the start, a look back at the finish. Here's one way to build yours. Morning, one minute: a preview, like Marcus. Who will I meet, where will it be hard, how do I want to be? Evening, one minute: pick one review. Maybe gratitude first, then one question, what did I mend or what did I leave undone, and end with the pardon. Two minutes a day in total. And like last week's breath routine, the version you'll actually keep beats the perfect one.
screen: `MORNING: MARCUS AT DAWN.` · `EVENING: FOUR REVIEWS.` · `THE DAY HELD AT BOTH ENDS.` · `ONE MINUTE EACH.` · then, large: `OPEN AND CLOSE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Do the morning bookend now, whatever the hour: preview what's left of today, who, where, and how you'd like to be. Then choose your evening review, gratitude first, one question, and the pardon, and picture yourself doing it tonight, lights out.
Bookends. A one-minute morning and a one-minute evening, so the day is held at both ends. Today's word.
Your line: open and close the day. Tomorrow a new week begins with Epictetus, and an old sorting question from philosophy. That's one hundred ten days.

howItsDone: Some people who keep a reflective practice hold the day at both ends: a short preview in the morning and a short review at night, drawn from sources like Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, the Golden Verses, the examen or Franklin's chart.
